title: Loaded Words
objective: After this level you can spot how word choice, like "used" versus "pre-owned", tilts a claim before any argument is made.
summary: Word choice can deliver a verdict before any argument: firm or pig-headed, used or pre-owned. Loaded language slips a value judgment into what looks like description.

cards.headline: "I am firm. You are obstinate. He is a pig-headed fool."
cards.body: Bertrand Russell offered this "conjugation" on the BBC radio program the Brains Trust, and in 1948 a magazine ran a contest for more. All three describe the same stubbornness. Only the verdict changes, and it arrives before anyone has given a reason.

cards.headline: Used, or pre-owned?
cards.body: Dictionaries define pre-owned simply as secondhand, or used. Same car, same mileage, gentler word. That's a euphemism: an agreeable word swapped in for one that sounds harsh or unpleasant. Nothing about the car changed on the lot. Only how you feel about it did.

cards.headline: Loaded language
cards.body: Loaded language is emotive wording that expresses a value judgment. Slipped into what looks like plain description, it can lead you to adopt that value when no good reason has been given. "The reckless new skate park opens Friday" reads like news. "Reckless" is a verdict riding along for free.

cards.headline: The neutral rewrite
cards.body: Here's the test: swap the loaded word for a neutral one and see what's left. "The new skate park opens Friday" is plain description. Whether the park is reckless is a separate claim, and now it has to earn its place with reasons, like any other value judgment.

mascot.line: It connects: a loaded word is Level 4's value judgment wearing a fact's clothes. Undress it and you can question it.

cards.headline: Loaded words: spotted
learned: Word choice can deliver a verdict before a reason
Loaded language hides a value judgment in description
Test it: swap in a neutral word

questions.prompt: Dictionaries give the meaning of "pre-owned" as _____.

options.label: nearly new, barely driven
options.rationale: Nothing in the word says how much it was used.

options.label: owned by one careful driver
options.rationale: It says nothing about who owned it.

questions.explanation: Pre-owned means secondhand: a gentler word for used.

questions.prompt: Complete Bertrand Russell's "conjugation": match each subject with its word.
questions.explanation: Russell's conjugation runs: I am firm, you are obstinate, he is a pig-headed fool. Same stubbornness, three verdicts.

questions.prompt: "The reckless new skate park opens Friday." What kind of claim does "reckless" add?

options.label: A factual claim about the opening
options.rationale: Opening on Friday is the fact; "reckless" is a verdict.

options.label: A matter of personal taste
options.rationale: It appeals to a standard of safety, not taste.

options.label: A question for the reader
options.rationale: It's a claim, not a question.

questions.explanation: "Reckless" measures the park against a standard: a value judgment riding inside a factual sentence.
